note: Hand-curated watchlist of accelerator-backed and breakout startups. Edit freely: add, remove, or bump `momentum`. Every entry is written to be *spoken*, not read.

companies.name: Pocket
companies.one_liner: A wearable note-taker that turns your conversations into action items.
companies.what_they_do: Pocket makes a small piece of hardware you clip on, paired with an app. It listens to your meetings and conversations and turns them into structured notes and action items, instead of a wall of transcript. Hardware plus software, sold direct to consumers.
companies.traction: Reported around twenty-seven million dollars in annual recurring revenue, over thirty thousand units shipped in about five months, and roughly fifty percent month-over-month growth. It was the revenue outlier of its entire batch.
companies.funding: Y Combinator Winter 2026 batch. Numbers reported around Demo Day in March 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: It is the loudest proof that AI hardware can go from zero to real revenue in months, not years, when the product does one obvious thing well.
companies.founder_angle: Notice they did not build a general assistant. They picked one moment - the meeting you just walked out of - and owned it end to end.

companies.name: Asimov
companies.one_liner: Real-world movement video used to train humanoid robots.
companies.what_they_do: Asimov collects and supplies video of humans doing real physical work, and sells it to robotics companies who need diverse, messy, real-world motion data to train humanoids. They are a picks-and-shovels business for the robot boom.
companies.traction: Named repeatedly by investors as one of the standouts of the Winter 2026 batch, in a batch where top valuations reached about two hundred million dollars post-money.
companies.why_it_matters: Everyone is racing to build humanoids. Almost nobody has the training data. Asimov sells to all sides of that race.
companies.founder_angle: The data bottleneck behind a hyped hardware wave is often a better business than the hardware.

companies.name: Hex Security
companies.one_liner: Autonomous agents that continuously attack your own systems, so you find the holes first.
companies.what_they_do: Hex Security runs agentic offensive security. Instead of hiring a pen-test firm once a year, you point their agents at your systems and they probe your defenses continuously, the way a real attacker would, and report what they broke.
companies.traction: One of only eight companies investors actively chased at the Winter 2026 Demo Day, according to TechCrunch.
companies.why_it_matters: Penetration testing has been a consulting business for thirty years. Agents turn it into software with software margins.
companies.founder_angle: Look for expensive services delivered once a year by humans. Those are the fattest targets for agents.

companies.name: Sazabi
companies.one_liner: Reads your production logs, works out why it broke, and ships the fix.
companies.what_they_do: When something breaks in production, Sazabi analyses the logs to find the cause, then generates the code fix and opens it for you in one click. It closes the loop between the alert and the patch.
companies.traction: Called out as a Winter 2026 standout by multiple investors.
companies.why_it_matters: Debugging production is where engineers actually lose their nights. This is the on-call engineer as a product.
companies.founder_angle: The winning agent products do not stop at the diagnosis. They deliver the fix.

companies.name: ARC Prize Foundation
companies.one_liner: The benchmark competition that measures real progress toward general intelligence.
companies.what_they_do: ARC Prize builds and runs benchmarks designed to test whether a model can genuinely reason on problems it has never seen, rather than recall training data. Frontier labs use their scores as a public scoreboard.
companies.traction: Reported to have crossed one hundred thousand monthly visitors, and used by teams including OpenAI.
companies.why_it_matters: Whoever defines the measuring stick quietly sets the agenda for the whole industry.
companies.founder_angle: Owning the scoreboard in a hyped field buys you distribution and credibility that money cannot.

companies.name: Pax Historia
companies.one_liner: Pick any country at any point in history and rewrite what happened.
companies.what_they_do: Pax Historia is a browser-based grand strategy game where the world reacts to you through AI rather than scripted rules. Choose a nation, choose a year, make a decision history never made, and the simulation plays it forward.
companies.traction: Around thirty-five thousand daily active users, and the highest-liked launch post of its entire batch, with over two thousand three hundred likes.
companies.why_it_matters: One of the very few genuinely consumer AI hits in a batch that was overwhelmingly business software.
companies.founder_angle: AI as the game engine, not the chatbot. The model generates the world, the player still plays a game.

companies.name: GRU Space
companies.one_liner: Permanent infrastructure on the Moon - including, eventually, a hotel.
companies.what_they_do: GRU Space is building the structures that stay on the lunar surface: habitats and permanent infrastructure rather than one-off landers. The headline version is a hotel on the Moon.
companies.traction: One of the eight companies investors chased hardest at Winter 2026 Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: A signal in itself. Investors are again funding twenty-year swings, not just software with revenue next quarter.
companies.founder_angle: An outrageous long-term vision still raises money, but only if the first milestone is unglamorous and concrete.

companies.name: GrazeMate
companies.one_liner: Autonomous drones that herd and monitor cattle.
companies.what_they_do: GrazeMate flies drones over grazing land to move cattle between paddocks and keep watch on the herd, replacing work that today needs people, dogs and quad bikes.
companies.traction: Among the eight most chased companies at Winter 2026 Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: Proof that the boring physical economy is where a lot of the remaining automation money sits.
companies.founder_angle: Ranching is not a sexy market. It is also a market where nobody has built decent software and the buyer feels the pain daily.

companies.name: Luel
companies.one_liner: A marketplace for human data to train multimodal models.
companies.what_they_do: Luel connects people willing to contribute video, audio and other human data with the labs that need it to train multimodal models. Think of it as a supply chain for the raw human signal models are running out of.
companies.traction: One of the eight companies investors chased at Winter 2026 Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: The public internet is exhausted as a training source. Fresh human data is now the scarce input.
companies.founder_angle: Same pattern as Asimov and Mercor. Marketplaces for scarce training inputs are the quiet winners of this cycle.

companies.name: Stilta
companies.one_liner: Agentic AI built specifically for patent and intellectual property attorneys.
companies.what_they_do: Stilta automates the document-heavy grind of IP and patent practice: drafting, prior art work, and office action responses, aimed at a profession that bills by the hour and drowns in paperwork.
companies.traction: One of the eight most chased startups at Winter 2026 Demo Day. Legal tech was among the fastest-growing categories in the batch.
companies.why_it_matters: Legal AI already produced Harvey and Legora as multi-billion-dollar companies. Patent law is the next unclaimed vertical.
companies.founder_angle: Go one layer deeper than the obvious vertical. Not legal - patent legal.

companies.name: Byteport
companies.one_liner: Absurdly fast file transfers.
companies.what_they_do: Byteport moves very large files between machines and clouds far faster than the standard tools, aimed at teams shifting datasets, model weights and video around all day.
companies.traction: Chased by investors at Winter 2026 Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: AI workloads made data movement a bottleneck again, and the incumbent tools were designed for a smaller era.
companies.founder_angle: Old, unglamorous infrastructure problems get new, large markets when the workload changes shape.

companies.name: Beyond Reach Labs
companies.one_liner: Giant solar panels for satellites.
companies.what_they_do: Beyond Reach Labs builds very large deployable solar arrays for spacecraft, so satellites and orbital compute can draw far more power than today's designs allow.
companies.traction: One of the eight companies investors chased at Winter 2026 Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: If anyone actually puts data centres in orbit, power generation is the first constraint they hit.
companies.founder_angle: Bet on the input a whole speculative industry will need, rather than on the speculative industry itself.

companies.name: Condor Energy
companies.one_liner: An operating system for how large companies buy and manage electricity.
companies.what_they_do: Condor gives enterprises one system to procure power and optimise how and when they generate and draw it, so electricity is cheaper, cleaner and more reliable.
companies.traction: Named a Winter 2026 standout by multiple investors.
companies.why_it_matters: Energy procurement went from a back-office line item to a board-level constraint the moment everyone started training models.
companies.founder_angle: When a cost line explodes, the software that manages that line becomes a category overnight.

companies.name: Milliray
companies.one_liner: Radar that can actually see small drones.
companies.what_they_do: Milliray builds radar systems tuned to detect and track small drones, the targets legacy air-defense radar was never designed to pick up.
companies.traction: Featured among the most interesting Winter 2026 companies. Counter-drone was one of the hottest themes across both 2026 batches.
companies.why_it_matters: Detection is the half of the counter-drone problem that has to be solved before any interceptor matters.
companies.founder_angle: In every hyped category, ask which unsexy half of the problem everyone is skipping.

companies.name: Librar Labs
companies.one_liner: AI library management for schools.
companies.what_they_do: Librar Labs handles cataloguing and inventory for school libraries, replacing decades-old systems that librarians hate and administrators never budget to replace.
companies.traction: Named among the most interesting Winter 2026 companies.
companies.why_it_matters: A reminder that small, ignored institutional markets still get funded when the software is obviously ten times better.
companies.founder_angle: You do not need a large market to start. You need a market where the current software is genuinely terrible.

companies.name: 9 Mothers
companies.one_liner: A cheap robot that tracks and kills drones flying at sixty miles an hour.
companies.what_they_do: 9 Mothers builds counter-drone interceptors: a physically small, relatively affordable robot that detects a hostile drone, tracks it, and takes it down, rather than firing a missile that costs more than the target.
companies.traction: Around one point six million dollars already booked in sales, with one contract expected to expand to thirty-five million dollars this year, and a claimed pipeline ambition of one billion dollars.
companies.funding: Investors chased it at a valuation upward of two hundred million dollars - the highest-valued company of the batch and one of the highest ever at a Y Combinator Demo Day.
companies.why_it_matters: The cost asymmetry of drone warfare is the defining defense problem of the decade, and this is the batch's clearest bet on it.
companies.founder_angle: The pitch was not better technology. It was a better unit cost against a threat that is already here.

companies.name: Apollo Atomics
companies.one_liner: Small modular nuclear reactors to power AI data centres.
companies.what_they_do: Apollo Atomics prefabricates reactor components so a nuclear plant can be assembled rather than constructed over twenty years. They physically shipped a demonstrator on a truck from Texas to California and showed it to about a dozen investors.
companies.traction: Twenty-four million dollar seed round, with Sam Altman among the backers. Founders include a nuclear science and engineering PhD from MIT and a former Tesla manufacturing engineer.
companies.funding: Twenty-four million dollar seed, Y Combinator Spring 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Power, not chips, is now the binding constraint on the AI build-out. Everyone knows it. Very few can actually build generation.
companies.founder_angle: They shipped a physical demonstrator to the meeting. In hard tech, the demo is the deck.

companies.name: Ploy
companies.one_liner: AI agents that run your growth marketing end to end.
companies.what_they_do: Ploy generates landing pages, writes the marketing copy, and launches and runs campaigns automatically. The explicit ambition is to make a large corporate marketing team unnecessary.
companies.traction: Twenty-seven million dollar seed round led by First Round Capital and Y Combinator - unusually large for a company just out of the batch.
companies.funding: Twenty-seven million dollar seed. Founded by Bryant Chou, co-founder and former chief technology officer of Webflow.
companies.why_it_matters: A repeat founder with a known outcome can raise a very large seed on the strength of the team alone in this market.
companies.founder_angle: Second-time founders skip the proving stage. If you are a first-timer, your traction has to do that work instead.

companies.name: Jedify
companies.one_liner: A context graph so AI agents actually understand how your business works.
companies.what_they_do: Jedify connects to a company's databases, warehouses, software tools, dashboards, documentation, code, Slack channels and meeting recordings, and builds a live graph of how the business actually operates, which agents then read from.
companies.traction: Twenty-four million dollar Series A, with Snowflake joining as a strategic investor.
companies.funding: Twenty-four million dollar Series A, announced June 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Agents fail in the enterprise for one boring reason: they do not know the company. Context is becoming its own infrastructure layer.
companies.founder_angle: The gap between a working demo and a working deployment is almost always context. That gap is a product.

companies.name: Silmaril
companies.one_liner: A firewall for AI agents that defends against prompt injection and retrains itself.
companies.what_they_do: Silmaril stops attackers from hijacking an agent through the text it reads - a poisoned email, a booby-trapped document, a malicious web page. Their system detects new attack patterns and retrains its own defenses as attacks evolve.
companies.traction: Repeatedly named a standout across the 2026 Y Combinator batches, in a year when AI security was one of the densest categories.
companies.why_it_matters: The moment agents can take real actions - send money, send email, run code - prompt injection stops being a curiosity and becomes the top enterprise blocker.
companies.founder_angle: Every platform shift creates a security category. This is that category for agents, and it is still early.

companies.name: Arga Labs
companies.one_liner: Digital-twin sandboxes where AI agents can test code before it touches production.
companies.what_they_do: Arga Labs spins up realistic copies of an enterprise's environment so agent-written code can be exercised safely and repeatedly. Testing has fallen far behind AI code generation, and this is the safety net.
companies.traction: Reported to have reached about forty thousand dollars in monthly recurring revenue within seven weeks, and raised a ten million dollar seed.
companies.funding: Ten million dollar seed, Y Combinator Spring 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: AI writes far more code than any team can review. The bottleneck moved from writing to verifying.
companies.founder_angle: When a new tool floods a pipeline, the next business is downstream of the flood.

companies.name: Clara
companies.one_liner: Reads your charts, labs, wearables and clinical notes and surfaces what matters now.
companies.what_they_do: Clara pulls together the fragments of a patient's record - chart history, lab results, wearable data, free-text clinical notes - and surfaces the important signals instantly instead of leaving them buried across systems.
companies.traction: Had already raised twelve million dollars before even entering the batch.
companies.funding: Twelve million dollars raised pre-batch. Y Combinator Spring 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Healthcare's most expensive failure is not diagnosis, it is information that existed but nobody saw in time.
companies.founder_angle: Some companies join an accelerator with money already in the bank. They are buying the network, not the cheque.

companies.name: Lightsprint
companies.one_liner: Product managers describe a change visually, cloud agents build it, an engineer approves it.
companies.what_they_do: Lightsprint lets a whole team - including non-engineers - plan visually, preview the result live, and ship. You say what you want changed, pick from visual options, an agent builds it, and an engineer reviews and merges the code.
companies.traction: Named among the buzziest companies of the Spring 2026 batch by multiple investors.
companies.why_it_matters: It keeps the engineer in the loop as the approver rather than removing them, which is what actually gets adopted inside real companies.
companies.founder_angle: The sellable version of 'AI replaces engineers' is 'AI drafts, your engineer approves'. Same output, far less resistance.

companies.name: Superset
companies.one_liner: Mission control for running a hundred coding agents at once.
companies.what_they_do: Superset centrally manages large fleets of coding agents, so a developer can run well over a hundred agent tasks in parallel and still know what each one is doing.
companies.traction: Named among the standout companies of Spring 2026 by investors.
companies.why_it_matters: One agent is a toy. A hundred agents is an operations problem, and operations problems are where durable software gets built.
companies.founder_angle: Whenever a unit becomes cheap and plentiful, the orchestration layer above it becomes valuable.

companies.name: Dispatch
companies.one_liner: A reusable vehicle that brings things manufactured in space back down to Earth.
companies.what_they_do: Dispatch is building the return leg of space manufacturing: a transport vehicle designed to be refurbished and flown repeatedly, carrying products made in orbit back to the ground.
companies.traction: Named among the Spring 2026 standouts, in a batch heavy on defense and space.
companies.why_it_matters: Several companies are trying to manufacture in orbit. Almost none have solved getting the product home affordably.
companies.founder_angle: Find the step everyone in an emerging industry assumes someone else will solve.

companies.name: Adialante
companies.one_liner: An MRI machine small enough to fit in a truck, at two hundred and fifty dollars a scan.
companies.what_they_do: Adialante has designed a compact MRI unit that can be transported in a small truck and driven to where patients are, with a business model built on charging around two hundred and fifty dollars per scan.
companies.traction: Named among the standouts of Spring 2026 by investors.
companies.why_it_matters: Imaging is gated by million-dollar machines in fixed buildings. Shrink the machine and the entire access model changes.
companies.founder_angle: Radical cost reduction is a strategy, not just an outcome. Price first, then design backwards to it.

companies.name: Anoria
companies.one_liner: A bracelet that reads over a hundred and fifty biometric signals for emotional health.
companies.what_they_do: Anoria is a wearable that tracks more than a hundred and fifty biometric signals and interprets them for emotional and mental health, rather than for fitness. It is led by a hardware founder out of Apple.
companies.traction: Named among the Spring 2026 standouts by investors.
companies.why_it_matters: Wearables have measured the body for a decade. Almost nobody has made the mind the product.
companies.founder_angle: Same sensors, different question. Reframing what existing hardware is for is a real wedge.

companies.name: SUN
companies.one_liner: Personalised podcasts and audiobooks you can interrupt and ask questions.
companies.what_they_do: SUN generates audio tailored to you - a podcast or audiobook built for your interests - and lets you talk back to it in real time, asking questions mid-listen and getting answers inside the same stream.
companies.traction: A three-person team out of Harvard computer science, a Stanford AI PhD, and the founding engineer of Amazon Podcasts. Selected into the a16z Speedrun sixth cohort.
companies.funding: a16z Speedrun invests up to one million dollars, plus up to five million dollars in credits.
companies.why_it_matters: This is precisely the format you are listening to right now, built as a company. Personalised, interruptible audio is a real emerging category.
companies.founder_angle: Worth watching closely if you ever want to build in this space - they are the closest competitor to your own daily brief.

companies.name: PicPet
companies.one_liner: A social network built around people's pets.
companies.what_they_do: PicPet is a social platform where the pet is the account. It is one of the few genuinely consumer companies in a Speedrun cohort that has become overwhelmingly business software.
companies.traction: Roughly two hundred and forty thousand daily active users, with about forty-five percent day-ninety retention - a genuinely strong retention number for consumer social.
companies.why_it_matters: Day-ninety retention near forty-five percent is the number that matters in consumer, and almost nobody hits it.
companies.founder_angle: In consumer, one retention number is worth more than any amount of growth narrative.

companies.name: Kaaro
companies.one_liner: An AI agent for the railway industry.
companies.what_they_do: Kaaro builds agents for rail operations - one of those enormous, deeply regulated, paperwork-heavy industries that almost no software founder ever looks at.
companies.traction: Selected into a16z Speedrun's sixth cohort, where eighty-seven percent of the sixty companies carried an AI tag and more than half were business-to-business.
companies.why_it_matters: Vertical agents in unglamorous heavy industry are one of the clearest patterns across every 2026 cohort.
companies.founder_angle: Pick an industry you have unfair access to. Domain access beats model access now.

companies.name: Vereda
companies.one_liner: AI procurement for agriculture, built out of Brazil.
companies.what_they_do: Vereda handles buying for farms and agricultural businesses - inputs, equipment, supply - with AI running the sourcing and negotiation work that today happens over phone calls and WhatsApp.
companies.traction: Selected into a16z Speedrun SR006, one of the international companies in an increasingly global cohort.
companies.why_it_matters: Top-tier American accelerators are now funding companies solving local problems in emerging markets, not just Silicon Valley software.
companies.founder_angle: Your local market's broken process is a fundable company, and you understand it better than anyone in San Francisco.

companies.name: Bilrost
companies.one_liner: Automates commercial loan processing.
companies.what_they_do: Bilrost takes the document-heavy grind of commercial lending - collecting statements, spreading financials, underwriting paperwork - and automates it for the banks and lenders who still do it by hand.
companies.traction: Selected into a16z Speedrun SR006. Roughly one third of that cohort published real revenue figures in their profiles.
companies.why_it_matters: Commercial lending is enormous, slow, and still runs on PDFs and email. That combination is the classic agent opportunity.
companies.founder_angle: Follow the PDF. Wherever an industry still emails documents around, there is a company.

companies.name: Ezra
companies.one_liner: The biggest tracked round to come out of the Speedrun portfolio this year.
companies.what_they_do: Ezra is the Speedrun alumnus that raised the largest tracked round in the portfolio recently, showing what the follow-on path out of the programme looks like when it works.
companies.traction: A thirty-two million dollar seed round in March 2026 - the largest tracked Speedrun deal.
companies.why_it_matters: Speedrun's whole thesis is being the first cheque before a much larger seed. Ezra is the proof point.
companies.founder_angle: Accelerators are increasingly graded on the size of the round that follows, not the demo day.

companies.name: Boardy
companies.one_liner: An AI that phones you, learns who you are, and introduces you to people worth meeting.
companies.what_they_do: Boardy is a voice agent you actually talk to. It interviews you about what you are working on and who you need, then makes warm introductions across its network - a super-connector that scales.
companies.traction: Named among HF0's most notable investments. HF0 writes one million dollar cheques for five percent, the largest single cheque among San Francisco accelerators.
companies.why_it_matters: Voice is the interface where AI feels least like software, and networking is a problem where a machine genuinely has more memory than you do.
companies.founder_angle: The product is a phone call. No app, no onboarding, no dashboard. Distribution built into the interface.

companies.name: Roofer.com
companies.one_liner: AI software for the roofing industry.
companies.what_they_do: Roofer.com brings AI-driven software to roofing contractors - quoting, lead handling, and the operational work of a trade business that has almost no modern software.
companies.traction: Cited as one of HF0's notable portfolio companies.
companies.why_it_matters: The trades are enormous, profitable, fragmented, and almost entirely un-softwared. Repeat founders are now deliberately choosing them.
companies.founder_angle: A great domain name plus a boring trade is a real strategy. Not everything has to be novel technology.

companies.name: Bastazo
companies.one_liner: Vulnerability management, pitched to Sequoia and Accel out of the HF0 residency.
companies.what_they_do: Bastazo works on vulnerability management - helping organisations work out which of the thousands of known security flaws in their systems actually matter and need fixing first.
companies.traction: Went through the HF0 residency and presented at its Demo Day to investors including Sequoia Capital and Accel.
companies.why_it_matters: Security teams are drowning in alerts. Prioritisation, not detection, is the unsolved half.
companies.founder_angle: HF0 takes repeat and highly technical founders in cohorts of about ten. Tiny cohort, huge cheque - a very different game from a big batch.

companies.name: Profound
companies.one_liner: Tells brands how they show up inside AI answers.
companies.what_they_do: Profound measures and shapes how a brand is represented when people ask AI assistants questions - the search-engine-optimisation problem rebuilt for a world where the answer comes from a model, not a list of links.
companies.traction: One of the companies most associated with the South Park Commons community, alongside Baseten, Render, Luma and Imbue.
companies.why_it_matters: If people stop clicking links, every marketing budget on earth has to be re-pointed at whatever this category becomes.
companies.founder_angle: When a distribution channel changes shape, the measurement layer for the new channel is a company.

companies.name: Mercor
companies.one_liner: A marketplace that pays human experts to train frontier models.
companies.what_they_do: Mercor matches domain experts - doctors, lawyers, bankers, engineers - with the AI labs that need their judgement to train and evaluate models. It is a labour marketplace pointed at model training.
companies.traction: Reported to have gone from about one million dollars to roughly two billion dollars in annualised gross revenue in around seventeen to twenty months, one of the fastest revenue ramps ever recorded.
companies.funding: Reported to be in talks to raise about five hundred million dollars at a twenty billion dollar valuation, up from ten billion in 2025.
companies.why_it_matters: The scarce input in AI is no longer compute or data. It is expert human judgement, and Mercor built the exchange for it.
companies.founder_angle: The fastest growth in this cycle came from a marketplace, not a model. Ask what the labs cannot buy anywhere else.

companies.name: Lovable
companies.one_liner: Describe an app in plain language and it builds and hosts it.
companies.what_they_do: Lovable turns a text description into a working web application - front end, back end, deployed - aimed at people who are not engineers. It is the flagship of what people call vibe coding.
companies.traction: Went from zero to about five hundred million dollars in annualised revenue in roughly fourteen months.
companies.funding: Confirmed a thirteen point three billion dollar valuation in August 2026, raising another four hundred million dollars, up from about six point six billion in December.
companies.why_it_matters: It is the clearest evidence that the buyer of software tools is shifting from engineers to everyone else.
companies.founder_angle: The market was never engineers who want to code faster. It was the far larger group who could never code at all.

companies.name: Cursor (Anysphere)
companies.one_liner: The AI code editor that became the fastest-growing business software company ever.
companies.what_they_do: Cursor is a code editor built around AI from the ground up, where the model reads your whole codebase and edits across it rather than autocompleting a line.
companies.traction: Reported as the fastest business software company in history to one billion dollars in annual recurring revenue, and then to two billion - ahead of Slack, Zoom and Snowflake at the same stage.
companies.funding: Reported valuation around sixty billion dollars.
companies.why_it_matters: It set the benchmark every developer-tools founder is now measured against, and it started as a small team competing with Microsoft.
companies.founder_angle: They rebuilt an existing tool around the new capability instead of bolting the new capability onto the old tool.

companies.name: Baseten
companies.one_liner: The plumbing that serves AI models in production.
companies.what_they_do: Baseten handles deploying, serving and scaling machine learning models, so a company can run inference reliably without building its own infrastructure team.
companies.traction: Reported total funding of around two point six billion dollars, backed by Greylock, Y Combinator and South Park Commons among others.
companies.funding: Valued at about thirteen billion dollars after a one point five billion dollar Series F led by Altimeter, Conviction and Spark Capital in June 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Inference is where the money in AI actually gets spent day to day, and Baseten sits directly in that flow.
companies.founder_angle: A Y Combinator company from 2019 that took six years to become obvious. Timing is a real risk, and patience is a real strategy.

companies.name: Mirendil
companies.one_liner: Autonomous systems that turn compute into scientific discoveries.
companies.what_they_do: Mirendil is a research lab building self-accelerating systems for science - AI that runs the research loop itself across fields like biology and materials science, rather than assisting a human researcher.
companies.traction: Founded in 2025 by Behnam Neyshabur, Harsh Mehta, Shayan Salehian and Tara Rezaei.
companies.funding: A two hundred million dollar seed round at a one billion dollar valuation, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia, Kleiner Perkins and Neo.
companies.why_it_matters: A two hundred million dollar seed at a billion-dollar valuation, on a research thesis with no product. That is the extreme end of this market.
companies.founder_angle: Reputation is now collateral. A team from the top of the research world can raise a Series B before writing a product.

companies.name: Sierra
companies.one_liner: AI agents that handle a company's customer conversations.
companies.what_they_do: Sierra builds branded customer-service agents that actually resolve issues - refunds, changes, troubleshooting - rather than deflecting to a help article. It was founded by Bret Taylor, now also chairman of OpenAI.
companies.traction: Reached one hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue in seven quarters, and about two hundred million in twenty-six months.
companies.funding: Reported valuation of roughly fifteen point eight billion dollars.
companies.why_it_matters: Customer service was the first big enterprise job that agents took outright, and Sierra is the template everyone copies.
companies.founder_angle: They charge per resolved issue rather than per seat. Pricing on outcomes is spreading fast across AI products.

companies.name: Harvey
companies.one_liner: AI built for elite law firms.
companies.what_they_do: Harvey does the research, drafting and document work inside large law firms and corporate legal departments, sold to the most conservative buyers in professional services.
companies.traction: Reported valuation around eleven billion dollars. Its success, alongside Legora, is why legal tech became one of the densest categories in the 2026 accelerator batches.
companies.funding: Reported at roughly an eleven billion dollar valuation.
companies.why_it_matters: Harvey proved that the most risk-averse industries will buy AI first if you sell it as leverage on billable work rather than as a replacement.
companies.founder_angle: High hourly rates plus repetitive document work equals the best AI market in the world. Now find the version nobody has claimed.

companies.name: Etched
companies.one_liner: A chip that does one thing - run transformers - and nothing else.
companies.what_they_do: Etched burns the transformer architecture directly into silicon. By giving up general-purpose flexibility, the bet is dramatically better speed and cost for the one model shape that matters commercially.
companies.traction: Reported as one of the two largest Series B rounds of 2026 at around five hundred million dollars.
companies.funding: Reported five hundred million dollar Series B.
companies.why_it_matters: It is a direct bet that the transformer stays dominant long enough to justify freezing it into hardware.
companies.founder_angle: The boldest strategies are subtractive. They removed flexibility on purpose and made that the product.

companies.name: Upscale AI
companies.one_liner: Networking hardware built for AI data centres.
companies.what_they_do: Upscale AI builds the networking layer that connects thousands of accelerators inside an AI data centre, where moving data between chips is now as much of a bottleneck as the chips themselves.
companies.traction: Raised a one hundred and ninety million dollar Series A extension, bringing total financing to about five hundred million dollars.
companies.funding: Reported valuation of around two billion dollars.
companies.why_it_matters: Every dollar of the data centre build-out drags networking spend behind it, and that layer has far fewer credible players than compute.
companies.founder_angle: Sell to the build-out, not to the hype. The suppliers get paid whether or not the applications work out.

companies.name: Replit
companies.one_liner: Build and deploy software from the browser, with an agent doing most of the typing.
companies.what_they_do: Replit is a browser-based environment where you describe what you want and an agent builds, runs and deploys it, with no local setup at all.
companies.traction: Reported growth from about two and a half million dollars to roughly five hundred and twenty-five million dollars in annualised revenue in around fourteen months.
companies.funding: One of the fastest companies to one hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue in 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: A decade-old developer tool that found a completely new and much larger market by adding an agent to what it already had.
companies.founder_angle: Distribution you already own plus a new capability can beat a new company with a better model.

companies.name: Unconventional AI
companies.one_liner: Chips designed like a brain, so AI stops burning a power station.
companies.what_they_do: Unconventional is a research lab building a new computing architecture for AI. Their observation is that AI models are probabilistic but the chips running them are not, so they are designing hardware that matches the maths - chasing something closer to the twenty watts a human brain runs on.
companies.traction: Chief executive Naveen Rao has sold two companies already: Nervana Systems to Intel for three hundred and fifty million dollars, and MosaicML to Databricks for one point three billion. Co-founders include Michael Carbin, Sara Achour and MeeLan Lee.
companies.funding: A four hundred and seventy-five million dollar seed round at a four point five billion dollar valuation, co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Lightspeed, with Lux Capital, DCVC and Jeff Bezos also in. Reported as the first tranche of a round that could reach one billion.
companies.why_it_matters: It is the largest seed round in this list by a distance, raised on a thesis and a founder's record, at a company only a couple of months old.
companies.founder_angle: Two exits bought him a four point five billion dollar valuation before a product existed. Track record is the only thing that compounds like that.

companies.name: Ornn
companies.one_liner: Turns GPU time into a commodity you can trade and hedge, like oil.
companies.what_they_do: Ornn is building a futures exchange for compute. Instead of privately negotiating a locked, long-term contract for a block of GPUs, you can price, trade, finance and hedge that capacity. Their price index covers live spot trades on H100, H200, B200 and RTX 5090 hardware.
companies.traction: The Ornn Compute Price Index is already distributed on the Bloomberg Terminal, and in May 2026 the Intercontinental Exchange announced a partnership to launch US dollar cash-settled GPU compute futures based on it.
companies.funding: A thirty-three million dollar seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz's crypto arm, with Galaxy Ventures, Nordstar and SV Angel joining.
companies.why_it_matters: Every commodity in history got a futures market once enough money depended on its price. Compute is now that big, and someone has to be the exchange.
companies.founder_angle: They did not build a better GPU cloud. They built the price index for everyone else's, and got it onto Bloomberg.

companies.name: Abridge
companies.one_liner: Listens to the doctor's appointment and writes the medical note.
companies.what_they_do: Abridge is ambient AI for clinicians. It sits in the room, listens to the conversation between doctor and patient, and produces the clinical documentation, so the doctor is not typing into a computer for hours after every shift.
companies.traction: The category leader in ambient clinical documentation, deployed across large American health systems.
companies.funding: A three hundred million dollar Series E led by Andreessen Horowitz and Khosla Ventures in April 2026, valuing it at five point three billion dollars, with a reported extension of a further three hundred and sixteen million.
companies.why_it_matters: Ambient documentation is the first AI product hospitals bought at scale, and it won because it gave time back rather than replacing anyone.
companies.founder_angle: Sell the hour back to the person who hates their paperwork. That buyer signs quickly and stays.

companies.name: Glimpse
companies.one_liner: Chases the money big retailers quietly deduct from consumer brands.
companies.what_they_do: When a supermarket chain pays a brand less than the invoice - a deduction for a damaged pallet, a late delivery, a promotion - somebody has to dispute it, line by line. Glimpse automates that deduction and dispute process for consumer packaged goods brands.
companies.traction: A Y Combinator company that pivoted into this, then raised a large Series A on the back of it.
companies.funding: A thirty-five million dollar Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, with 8VC and Y Combinator participating, announced March 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: An unglamorous back-office leak with real money in it, in an industry where the incumbent process is a spreadsheet and a phone call.
companies.founder_angle: This is a pivot story. The company that raised the Series A is not the company that got into the batch.

companies.name: Saronic
companies.one_liner: Autonomous boats, built in America, at a price the navy can buy in numbers.
companies.what_they_do: Saronic builds uncrewed surface vessels - autonomous boats for naval missions, designed to be produced in volume rather than as bespoke million-dollar craft.
companies.traction: One of the flagship companies of Andreessen Horowitz's American Dynamism practice, alongside Anduril.
companies.funding: Reported to have raised a one hundred and seventy-five million dollar Series B at a one billion dollar valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz.
companies.why_it_matters: Andreessen Horowitz raised about one point two billion dollars for American Dynamism alone in January 2026. Defense manufacturing is now a core venture category, not a curiosity.
companies.founder_angle: Same lesson as 9 Mothers, at a bigger scale: in defense, cheap and many beats exquisite and few.

companies.name: Anduril
companies.one_liner: The company that proved a startup could sell serious weapons systems.
companies.what_they_do: Anduril builds autonomous defense systems - surveillance towers, drones, counter-drone systems, and the software layer that ties them together - and sells them as products rather than as decade-long cost-plus programmes.
companies.traction: The anchor company of the whole defense tech wave, and the reason a batch of 2026 accelerator companies could raise money on counter-drone and autonomy pitches at all.
companies.funding: A long-standing Andreessen Horowitz position and the firm's most-cited American Dynamism company.
companies.why_it_matters: Every defense company in this brief is, in some sense, pitching investors on being early Anduril.
companies.founder_angle: One company changing what investors believe is possible opens the door for a hundred more. Being second into a proven category is much easier than being first.

companies.name: Ambience Healthcare
companies.one_liner: Ambient AI that documents the visit and gets the billing code right.
companies.what_they_do: Ambience listens to clinical encounters and produces documentation, with a heavy focus on coding and compliance - the part that decides whether the hospital actually gets paid correctly for the visit.
companies.traction: Reported to have raised a two hundred and forty-three million dollar Series C led by Oak HC slash FT, competing directly with Abridge.
companies.funding: Two hundred and forty-three million dollar Series C, reported.
companies.why_it_matters: Two very well-funded companies in the same category, differentiating on revenue capture rather than transcription quality.
companies.founder_angle: When a category has an obvious leader, the wedge is usually the adjacent workflow the leader treats as secondary.

companies.name: Hippocratic AI
companies.one_liner: Voice AI agents that call patients and do the nursing follow-up.
companies.what_they_do: Rather than transcribing a visit, Hippocratic builds patient-facing voice agents: intake calls, pre-operation checks, chronic care check-ins and inpatient nursing support, in a category where a mistake has real consequences.
companies.traction: Described as the clear category leader in patient-facing AI agents, reportedly valued around three point five billion dollars, up from one point six four billion at its Series B.
companies.funding: A one hundred and forty-one million dollar Series B led by Kleiner Perkins, with a later valuation reported at about three point five billion dollars.
companies.why_it_matters: It is the most aggressive test anywhere of whether an AI agent can be trusted to speak directly to a patient.
companies.founder_angle: They priced by the hour of nursing work delivered, not by software seat. In healthcare, match the buyer's existing budget line.

companies.name: Keythorn
companies.one_liner: Insurance for the new risks that appear when agents act on your behalf.
companies.what_they_do: Keythorn is underwriting the risks created as AI agents enter the economy. When an agent books, buys, files or acts wrongly, somebody carries that liability - and right now almost nobody has priced it.
companies.traction: In the seventh Speedrun cohort, which is running right now: it started on 27 July and its Demo Day is 6 October 2026. Details are thin by design at this stage.
companies.funding: a16z Speedrun invests up to one million dollars, plus up to five million in credits.
companies.why_it_matters: Insurance is how a new technology becomes legally deployable at scale. This is a bet on being early to that.
companies.founder_angle: Ask what breaks legally and financially when the hyped thing works. That question is a company.

companies.name: Phyvant
companies.one_liner: AI that learns how your staff actually get things done, not how the manual says.
companies.what_they_do: Phyvant builds procedural memory for the enterprise - capturing the real sequence of steps employees follow to do a job, so an agent can repeat it rather than improvise from a document.
companies.traction: Part of the Speedrun SR007 cohort now in progress, with Demo Day on 6 October 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Same insight as Jedify from a different angle: the missing ingredient for enterprise agents is knowledge that was never written down.
companies.founder_angle: Two funded companies attacking enterprise context from opposite ends is a signal, not a coincidence. That is where the market is.

companies.name: ELU
companies.one_liner: Software that repairs itself.
companies.what_they_do: ELU is working on self-healing software - systems that detect their own failures and fix them without a human in the loop, the logical end point of what Sazabi does one step at a time.
companies.traction: In the Speedrun SR007 cohort currently running, Demo Day 6 October 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: If code can write itself, the next question is whether it can maintain itself. Several teams are now betting yes.
companies.founder_angle: Watch what the newest cohort is building. It is the closest thing to a live feed of what smart people think is now possible.

companies.name: Bounty
companies.one_liner: A marketplace where agents hire other agents.
companies.what_they_do: Bounty is building an agent marketplace - a place where a task can be posted and picked up by whichever agent can do it, rather than every company wiring every capability itself.
companies.traction: Speedrun SR007, currently in programme.
companies.why_it_matters: Marketplaces only work once supply is plentiful and interchangeable. Somebody has decided agents just crossed that line.
companies.founder_angle: Marketplace timing is everything. Too early and there is no supply; too late and someone owns the demand.

companies.name: OpenWhispr
companies.one_liner: Voice as the way you drive software.
companies.what_they_do: OpenWhispr is building voice AI tooling - dictation and speech control aimed at making talking a first-class way to operate a computer rather than a novelty.
companies.traction: Speedrun SR007, Demo Day 6 October 2026.
companies.why_it_matters: Voice keeps almost working. Every cycle, transcription gets good enough that somebody rebuilds the interface layer on top.
companies.founder_angle: Relevant to how you are consuming this brief. Audio-first interfaces are having a genuine moment.

companies.name: Kira
companies.one_liner: Water technology, in a cohort otherwise full of software.
companies.what_they_do: Kira is the water technology company in the current Speedrun batch - one of the few in a cohort where the overwhelming majority carry an AI tag and more than half sell to businesses.
companies.traction: Speedrun SR007, currently running.
companies.why_it_matters: Data centres consume enormous quantities of water. Water and power are becoming the same conversation.
companies.founder_angle: Being the only one of your kind in a cohort is a position, not a problem. You are the memorable pitch in the room.
